ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating the Performance of Off-the-Shelf LLMs for Time Series Quality Assessment
PROPOSAL: Train a set of off-the-shelf LLMs (e.g. T5, BART, and a transformer-based encoder-decoder in the style of the ones in the Longformer family) on various time series tasks (forecasting and classification) to generate quality assessments for diverse real-world time series datasets (e.g. M5, ExchangeRateDataset, and Traffic Forecasting)^*. Evaluate their performance against state-of-the-art time series data quality estimation methods (TimeInf and TimeShap), and measure the scores for both accuracy and efficiency.
CONTROLS: Baseline against TimeInf and TimeShap, ablation study on model architecture and task
COST: 1000
PREDICTION: These models are expected to significantly underperform state-of-the-art methods for time series data quality assessment, particularly due to their default to using encoding representations commonly used for generic text generation and lack of domain-specific knowledge. However, they might show acceptable performance on traffic forecasting where short-term trend patterns are non-stationary but relatively predictable and have been taught using little in-domain training, specially given LLM's versatility on diverse linguistic inputs.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Designing Effective Prompts for Time Series Data Quality Assessment using LLMs
PROPOSAL: Experiment with various carefully designed prompts (to elicit specific attributes of time series such as smoothness, seasonality, or trends) for guiding LLMs (e.g. T5, BART) to generate accurate quality assessments for time series data. Evaluate the performance of different prompt types (e.g. template-based, question-answer, and text-based) on real-world datasets (electricity load forecasting, exchange rate forecasting, and traffic forecasting), and use techniques such as active learning and reinforcement learning to adapt and refine the prompts.
CONTROLS: Evaluation of off-the-shelf LLMs proposed in experiment 1, ablation study on prompt types
COST: 1200
PREDICTION: LLMs can be effectively guided with tailored prompts to rate time series quality with a reasonable level of accuracy, but optimal prompts for a specific time series characteristics and tasks would be hard to obtain. For instance, things might fail for very simple time series evaluation cases that require expert human knowledge close to subtle interconnected nuances.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Training Time Series Foundation Models with Auxiliary Loss Functions for Data Quality Estimation
PROPOSAL: Adapt the architecture of LLMs (e.g. transformer-based encoder-decoders) for training with auxiliary loss functions (e.g. mean squared error, classification cross-entropy) on time series data to enable them to predict quality scores. Train the models on large-scale time series corpora (electricity load forecasting, exchange rate forecasting, and traffic forecasting) and evaluate their performance on unseen data from diverse domains, using metrics such as precision, recall, and F1 score.
CONTROLS: Baseline against LLMs trained without auxiliary loss functions, comparison with TimeInf and TimeShap
COST: 1800
PREDICTION: These models are expected to outperform traditional methods (TimeInf and TimeShap) in many cases, particularly on heavily pre-trained models like Longformer's due to foundation of semantic content generalizable across text subdomains but struggle with cases requiring a deep 'human' intuition for specific characteristics till ground-truth examples are available due to broad, shallow coverage.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Revising Training Time Series Foundation Models with Auxiliary Loss Functions for Data Quality Estimation
PROPOSAL: To tackle potential cases where foundation models focus on predicting outputs which bring them close to expected quality labels but neglect learning accurate time series model capacity: Incorporate a secondary (debit) task loss during training that penalizes when model-final quality predictions significantly vary from continuous segment-level quality labels obtained from human annotators or even as evaluated indirectly through back passes from a polished pre-existing time series model. This secondary loss aims to maintain acceptable time series modeling properties through trained quality estimators along with originally imposed quality scoring requirements.
CONTROLS: comparison of performance on given debit task layer during training, additional impact analysis of a higher debit task loss weights
COST: 2000
PREDICTION: This augmented training regime improves the models' capacity to maintain predicted quality scores while accomplishing quality measurements with an acceptable fixed model, reducing common drawbacks for utilizing model outputs for coarse, large-scale data screening tasks. However, the added computational requirement of the debit task may reveal some implementation challenges and even limitations when architecting future versions of this method.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Understanding the Time Series Representation Learned by LLMs for Quality Assessment
PROPOSAL: Analyze the internal representations learned by LLMs for time series quality assessment tasks (specifically attention weights, encoder-decoder outputs, and contextual embeddings) to uncover patterns and mechanisms underlying their decision-making process. Use interpretability techniques (e.g. SALib, LRP, Integrated Gradients) and visualization methods (e.g. t-SNE, PCA) to identify key features, attributes, or relationships that contribute to the models' quality assessments.
CONTROLS: Baseline against random guessing, comparison with human annotations
COST: 1300
PREDICTION: LLMs will learn a combination of both domain-agnostic and domain-specific features to represent time series for quality assessment, with a focus on those that are highly discriminative for quality scores, and some form of spatial hierarchy of attention weights indicating order was being somewhat optimized along short temporal subintervals, aiding the quality evaluation of time series.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Robustness of LLM-based Time Series Quality Assessment to Data Distribution Shifts
PROPOSAL: Evaluate the robustness of LLMs trained for time series quality assessment to distribution shifts in time series data (e.g. changes in seasonality, signal magnitude, or sampling rates). Use transfer learning and data augmentation techniques (e.g. mixing time series datasets, injecting noise) to assess the models' ability to generalize across different domains and environments. Compare their performance with traditional methods (TimeInf and TimeShap) and discuss implications for real-world applications.
CONTROLS: Baseline against LLMs trained without transfer learning/data augmentation, comparison with human annotations
COST: 1600
PREDICTION: LLMs will show some level of robustness to moderate changes in time series data distribution due to their large-scale training on diverse text domains but are likely to struggle significantly with larger-scale distribution shifts. Some initial deployments to validating traffic forecasting demonstrated probabilities being weakened by scores of certain variation scenarios, failing under broader testing conditions.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Exploring the Use of Adversarial Training for Improving LLM-based Time Series Quality Assessment
PROPOSAL: Adapt the training procedure for LLMs to incorporate adversarial perturbations (e.g. using time series data augmentation) that aim to mislead the models into providing incorrect quality assessments. Train the LLMs with an additional adversarial loss (e.g. using a discriminator networks) to improve their robustness and accuracy. Evaluate the performance of adversarially trained LLMs on a range of time series quality assessment tasks and compare them with state-of-the-art methods (TimeInf and TimeShap).
CONTROLS: Baseline against LLMs trained without adversarial training, comparison with human annotations
COST: 2200
PREDICTION: Adversarially trained LLMs will demonstrate improved robustness to various forms of time series data attacks, including distribution shifts, outliers, and noise, but may also lead to overfitting, higher latency during testing and potential enhance computational costs of model use. Perhaps testing a range of perturbation possibilities would produce acceptable performance levels atop "blackboxing" attacks more frequently deployed.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Combining LLM-based and Traditional Methods for Enhanced Time Series Data Quality Assessment
PROPOSAL: Investigate the benefits of combining LLM-based quality assessment methods with traditional approaches (TimeInf and TimeShap) to leverage their respective strengths. Experiment with different combination strategies (e.g., ensemble methods, stacking, and fusion) to evaluate their impact on overall quality assessment performance. Evaluate the performance of combined methods on a range of time series quality assessment tasks and compare them with state-of-the-art methods.
CONTROLS: Baseline against individual LLM-based and traditional methods, ablation study on combination strategies
COST: 1800
PREDICTION: The combination of LLM-based and traditional methods will lead to improved quality assessment performance, particularly in cases where LLMs struggle with domain-specific characteristics. However, optimal combination strategies may depend on the specific time series domain and quality assessment task, requiring further investigation.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Deployment and Evaluation of LLM-based Time Series Data Quality Assessment in Real-World Scenarios
PROPOSAL: Deploy LLM-based time series data quality assessment methods in real-world scenarios, such as electricity load forecasting, exchange rate forecasting, and traffic forecasting, to evaluate their performance in practical settings. Collect real-world data, assess the quality of the data, and compare the performance of LLM-based methods with traditional approaches. Identify challenges and opportunities for improving the deployment of LLM-based methods in real-world scenarios.
CONTROLS: Baseline against traditional methods, evaluation of LLM-based methods on real-world data
COST: 2600
PREDICTION: LLM-based time series data quality assessment methods will demonstrate strong performance in real-world scenarios, particularly in domains where they have been pre-trained on large amounts of data. However, challenges such as data quality issues, distribution shifts, and domain adaptation may hinder their performance, requiring further investigation and adaptation.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Theoretical Analysis of LLM-based Time Series Data Quality Assessment
PROPOSAL: Provide a theoretical foundation for LLM-based time series data quality assessment by analyzing the properties and limitations of these models. Investigate the generalization error of LLMs in the context of time series data quality assessment, and provide bounds on their performance. Explore the impact of model architecture, training data, and evaluation metrics on the quality of LLM-based time series data quality assessment.
CONTROLS: Rigorous mathematical analysis, evaluation of theoretical results against empirical findings
COST: 3300 ( highest due to the rigorous mathematical requirements to derive solid theory )
PREDICTION: The theoretical analysis will reveal that LLMs are capable of providing accurate time series data quality assessments, but their performance is limited by their capacity to handle complex time series relationships and noisy data. Optimal model architecture, training data, and evaluation metrics will be identified, but strict conditions on training and test data quality will also be established.

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Evaluating the Impact of Model Size on Adversarial Anonymization Performance
PROPOSAL: We will compare the performance of我们的 adversarial anonymization on three different model sizes (T5-small, T5-base, T5-large) using a synthetic dataset where authors' location is inferred from online comments. The goal is to understand whether smaller models can achieve comparable anonymization performance to larger models, reducing compute requirements and deployment complexity. We will evaluate the models on standard metrics like F1-score and AUPRC, comparing their ability to prevent adversary from inferring correct locations. 
CONTROLS:  baseline of using no anonymization, baseline of GPT-4 as anonymizer
COST: 10000
PREDICTION: We expect smaller models to struggle to achieve the same level of anonymization performance as the large T5 model, but T5-base may still offer a good privacy-utility trade-off while requiring less compute than the large model; the results could fail if either smaller models perform surprisingly well or if there are significant batch effects in the dataset.

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Adversarial Training with Synthetic Adversarial Examples
PROPOSAL: To further improve the robustness of our anonymizer, we will implement adversarial training where the anonymizer is trained to withstand adversarial examples generated using multiple common text manipulation techniques (backtranslation, word substitution, deleting or adding random words). We will use a synthetic dataset where authors' demographics are tweaked to create adversarial examples, and evaluate the performance of the anonymizer on these examples. Our goal is to understand whether this approach can enhance anonymization performance and make our system more resistant to evasion attacks. 
CONTROLS: baseline of standard training without adversarial examples, comparison to state-of-the-art LLMs on this task
COST: 12000
PREDICTION: We expect to see a significant improvement in the anonymizer's performance on adversarial examples, which could fail if the synthetic adversarial examples are not representative of real-world attacks or if the model becomes overly specialized to a specific set of adversarial techniques.

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Quality-Efficiency Trade-off of Few-Shot Anonymization
PROPOSAL: Given the limited data availability for training local anonymizers, we will explore the feasibility of few-shot anonymization, where the anonymizer is fine-tuned on a small dataset (e.g., 10% of the full training set). We will evaluate the quality-efficiency trade-off of few-shot anonymization on a range of few-shot learning settings (5, 10, 20 examples), testing the anonymizer's ability to preserve semantic meaning and prevent adversary inference. Our goal is to understand whether few-shot anonymization can offer a reasonable privacy-utility trade-off under limited training data. 
CONTROLS: baseline of standard training on full dataset, state-of-the-art few-shot learning methods without anonymization
COST: 15000
PREDICTION: We expect to see a noticeable decline in anonymizer performance when using few-shot learning, but also a discoverable sweet spot where precision and recall balance out against training time; the results could fail if the few-shot learning setting induces unintended regularization effects or if the synthetic dataset doesn't accurately capture real-world data sparsity.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Quality-Efficiency Trade-off of Few-Shot Anonymization
PROPOSAL: Given the limited data availability for training local anonymizers, we will explore the feasibility of few-shot anonymization, where the anonymizer is fine-tuned on a small dataset (e.g., 10% of the full training set). We will evaluate the quality-efficiency trade-off of few-shot anonymization using a subset of adversarially-trained inputs from proposal 2, testing the anonymizer's ability to preserve semantic meaning and prevent adversary inference under limited training data and against stronger attacks. Our goal is to understand whether few-shot anonymization can offer a reasonable privacy-utility trade-off when real-world adversarial threats are considered. 
CONTROLS: baseline of standard training on full dataset, state-of-the-art few-shot learning methods without anonymization
COST: 18000
PREDICTION: We expect to see an even more pronounced decline in anonymizer performance when using few-shot learning, especially when considering adversarial examples, but also a discoverable sweet spot where precision and recall balance out against training time; the results could fail if the few-shot learning setting induces particularly severe degradation or if the dataset does not generalise to stronger adversarial threats.

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Anonymizer-Agnostic Adversarial Attacks
PROPOSAL: To further stress-test the robustness of our anonymizer, we will design anonymizer-agnostic adversarial attacks that focus on manipulating the input text in a way that evades anonymization, rather than directly targeting the content. We will train a separate model on a dataset of original text and corresponding anonymized text, and use it to generate adversarial examples that are maximally different from the original text while still being anonymized. Our goal is to evaluate how well our anonymizer performs against these attacks and identify potential vulnerabilities. 
CONTROLS: baseline of standard anonymizer performance on random noise inputs, comparison to state-of-the-art LLMs on this task
COST: 22000
PREDICTION: We expect to see a significant increase in the efficacy of these anonymizer-agnostic attacks, potentially leading to breakthroughs in evasion techniques; the results could fail if the anonymous examples are not robust against inference attacks or if the anonymizer's security holds against such attacks despite their design.

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Understanding Anonymizer Robustness using Sensitivity Analysis
PROPOSAL: To better understand the robustness of our anonymizer, we will perform sensitivity analysis on a range of input factors (e.g. text length, author expertise, an original post's context). We will evaluate how changes in these factors affect the anonymizer's performance, in order to pinpoint vulnerabilities and potential biases in the system. Our goal is to identify potential limitations of the anonymizer and inform potential improvements. 
CONTROLS: baseline of standard anonymizer performance on original dataset, comparison to sensitivity analysis on state-of-the-art LLMs
COST: 26000
PREDICTION: We expect to identify a range of factors that can compromise the anonymizer's security, such as sensitive text features, anomalous input patterns, or characteristics that affect the adversary's confidence; the results could fail if the sensitivity analysis does not identify robust vulnerabilities in the anonymizer.

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Quantifying Information Disclosure through Reverse Engineering
PROPOSAL: To further assess the potential risks of using our anonymizer, we will perform a reverse engineering analysis on the anonymized text to quantify the amount of information that is still disclosed despite anonymization. We will use techniques from program analysis and information theory to measure the leakage of sensitive information, such as author demographics or location. Our goal is to provide a more comprehensive understanding of the anonymizer's security guarantees and potential limitations. 
CONTROLS: baseline of original text information, comparison to similar analysis on state-of-the-art LLMs
COST: 30000
PREDICTION: We expect to find that our anonymizer does not perfectly eliminate information disclosure, and identify specific mechanisms through which sensitive information can still be inferred; the results could fail if the reverse engineering analysis is too narrowly focused or if it does not uncover meaningful vulnerabilities.

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Empirical Analysis of Anonymizer Transferability Across Domains
PROPOSAL: To better understand the generalizability of our anonymizer across different text domains (e.g., social media, forums, product reviews), we will conduct an empirical analysis of anonymizer transferability. We will evaluate the performance of our anonymizer on a range of text datasets from different domains and compare it to state-of-the-art LLMs. Our goal is to identify potential pitfalls and opportunities for fine-tuning the anonymizer for specific domains. 
CONTROLS: baseline of standard anonymizer performance on a single domain, comparison to similar analysis on state-of-the-art LLMs across multiple domains
COST: 32000
PREDICTION: We expect to see a noticeable decline in anonymizer performance when using it across domains different from its original training dataset, but also identify some latent transferability that can be optimized through fine-tuning; the results could fail if the anonymizer performs surprisingly poorly or if it exhibits significant biases towards certain domains.

ACTION: REVISE 7
TITLE: Empirical Analysis of Anonymizer Transferability Across Domains
PROPOSAL: To further refine our understanding of anonymizer transferability, we will explore the usage of adversarial training with domain-incremental learning (ADV-DIL) to improve anonymizer performance across different text domains. This approach involves fine-tuning the anonymizer on a small dataset from a target domain while adapting to the domain-specific features and vulnerabilities. Our goal is to push the performance limits of anonymizer transferability and determine whether ADV-DIL can solve domain adaptation for anonymizers. 
CONTROLS: baseline of standard anonymizer performance on a single domain, state-of-the-art domain adaptation methods for LLMs on this task, comparison to ADV-DIL without fine-tuning
COST: 36000

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Scalable and Generic Anonymization Pipeline for Inference-based Privacy Threats
PROPOSAL: To demonstrate the practicality and effectiveness of our anonymizer, we will develop a scalable and generic anonymization pipeline that can be easily integrated with existing text processing systems. We will implement a modular architecture that allows for the seamless integration of different anonymization strategies (e.g., rewriting, masking, and tokenization) and provide a user-friendly interface for configuring and fine-tuning the pipeline. Our goal is to showcase the anonymizer's potential for real-world deployment and scalability. 
CONTROLS: baseline of standard anonymizer performance on a range of text datasets, comparison to state-of-the-art text anonymization systems
COST: 40000
PREDICTION: We expect to see a significant reduction in deployment complexity and an improvement in the overall performance of the anonymizer, setting the stage for large-scale real-world adoption and impact; the results could fail if the pipeline is not easily scalable or if it induces unintended biases.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Non-Asymptotic Bounds for KernelSHAP
PROPOSAL: Develop non-asymptotic sample-complexity guarantees for KernelSHAP, the most widely used randomized estimator for computing Shapley values, by analyzing its statistical properties and providing a theoretical framework for understanding its performance. Specifically, derive a bound on the mean squared error (MSE) of KernelSHAP's output in terms of the number of subsampled rows, the variance of the sampling distribution, and the condition number of the regression problem.
CONTROLS: Analyze existing versions of KernelSHAP, LeverangeSHAP and SHAP library implementation.
COST: 4800
PREDICTION: We expect to obtain a non-asymptotic bound with a dependence on the number of features, which can provide insight into KernelSHAP's scalability, but the bound might not be tight, leading to a potential mismatch between theory and practice.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Empirical Evaluation of Sampling Distributions for Estimators of Shapley Values
PROPOSAL: Conduct an empirical study to compare the performance of different sampling distributions in estimators of Shapley values, including KernelSHAP's original sampling distribution, unbiased KernelSHAP, and LeverageSHAP. This study aims to provide insights into which sampling distribution is most effective in practice and to shed light on the design of more efficient estimators.
CONTROLS: Compare to baseline of KernelSHAP and unbiased KernelSHAP without changing the sampling distribution.
COST: 21600
PREDICTION: We expect to see that the choice of sampling distribution has a significant impact on the accuracy of Shapley value estimates, with LeverageSHAP's sampling distribution performing particularly well, but we might encounter issues with the computational efficiency of some estimators in high-dimensional data.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: High-Dimensional Estimation of Shapley Values using Gradient Descent
PROPOSAL: Propose a novel algorithm for estimating Shapley values in high-dimensional settings by formulating the problem as a constrained optimization task and applying gradient descent. This approach avoids the need for exhaustive subset enumeration, making it potentially more efficient than existing methods.
CONTROLS: Compare to subset-based method (e.g. SimSHAP) for fixed computational budget.
COST: 51840
PREDICTION: We expect the algorithm to achieve a good trade-off between computational efficiency and estimation accuracy, but it may not outperform existing methods in terms of Hellinger distance to the exact Shapley values, and its convergence properties might require further investigation.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: High-Dimensional Estimation of Shapley Values using Gradient Descent
PROPOSAL: REVISED PROPOSAL: Investigate the use of stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with a customized learning rate schedule to improve the estimation accuracy and computational efficiency of the high-dimensional estimation algorithm. In particular, analyze the convergence properties of SGD in this context and provide a theoretical guarantee on the number of iterations required to achieve a desired level of accuracy.
CONTROLS: As before, compare to subset-based method (e.g. SimSHAP) for fixed computational budget.
COST: 51840
PREDICTION: With the revised proposal, we expect to be able to achieve faster convergence and better accuracy, but the customized learning rate schedule might require careful tuning to avoid over-shooting or under-shooting the optimal solution.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Shapley Values for Deep Neural Networks using Layer-wise Explanations
PROPOSAL: Develop a method for estimating Shapley values for deep neural networks by decomposing the network into individual layers and applying layer-wise explanations to approximate the Shapley values. This approach can help alleviate the computational challenges of estimating Shapley values for large and complex models.
CONTROLS: Evaluate on image and tabular datasets using a variety of deep neural network architectures.
COST: 129600
PREDICTION: We expect the method to be computationally efficient and scalable to large models, but the accuracy of the Shapley value estimates might depend on the quality of the layer-wise explanations, and there may be challenges in interpreting the results for complex models.

ACTION: REVISE 4
TITLE: Shapley Values for Deep Neural Networks using Layer-wise Explanations
PROPOSAL: REVISED PROPOSAL: Investigate the use of model-agnostic explanations, such as LIME or Anchor, as an intermediate step to estimate the importances of features with respect to each layer, and then use these importances to approximate the Shapley values. This revised approach can combine the strengths of different explanation techniques and provide a more comprehensive understanding of the model's behavior.
CONTROLS: Evaluate on image and tabular datasets using a variety of deep neural network architectures, compare to original proposal.
COST: 194592
PREDICTION: With the revised proposal, we expect to be able to leverage the strengths of multiple explanation techniques, but the accuracy of the Shapley value estimates might depend on the quality of the intermediate explanations, and there may be challenges in scaling the method to very large models.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Towards Provably Efficient Estimation of Shapley Values in High Dimensions
PROPOSAL: Investigate the use of statistical learning theory to develop a new estimator for Shapley values that is provably efficient in high-dimensional settings. Specifically, design an estimator that achieves a near-optimal trade-off between sample complexity and approximation accuracy, and provide a theoretical analysis of its guarantees.
CONTROLS: Compare to existing estimators, such as KernelSHAP and LeverageSHAP, on both synthetic and real-world datasets.
COST: 345600
PREDICTION: We expect the new estimator to achieve significant improvements in terms of sample efficiency and approximation accuracy, but its practical performance might depend on the choice of hyperparameters and the difficulty of the problem instance.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Analysis of Uncertainty in Shapley Value Estimation
PROPOSAL: Investigate the propagation of uncertainty in Shapley value estimation, including the sources of uncertainty and their impact on the accuracy of Shapley value estimates. This analysis will help to identify the limitations of current estimation methods and provide a framework for developing more robust and reliable Shapley value estimators.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the sensitivity of Shapley value estimates to model choice, hyperparameters, and data noise on a range of real-world datasets.
COST: 518400
PREDICTION: We expect to identify several sources of uncertainty in Shapley value estimation, including model uncertainty and data noise, and provide insights into their impact on the accuracy of Shapley value estimates, but the analysis might be computationally intensive and require careful tuning of hyperparameters.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Scalable Implementation of Shapley Value Estimation for Large-Scale Machine Learning
PROPOSAL: Develop a scalable and efficient implementation of Shapley value estimation for large-scale machine learning models, including distributed and parallel computing frameworks, to enable the estimation of Shapley values for complex models and large datasets.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the performance of the implementation on a range of large-scale machine learning models and datasets, comparing to existing implementations.
COST: 1036800
PREDICTION: We expect the implementation to achieve significant speedups and make Shapley value estimation feasible for large-scale machine learning models, but the development of a robust and efficient implementation might require significant engineering efforts and careful consideration of parallelization and distributed computing strategies.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Case Studies of Shapley Value Estimation in Real-World Applications
PROPOSAL: Conduct a series of case studies to demonstrate the effectiveness of Shapley value estimation in real-world applications, including but not limited to, explainable recommendations, fairness auditing, and model debugging. These case studies will provide concrete examples of how Shapley value estimation can be used to gain insights into complex systems and inform decision-making processes.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the usefulness of Shapley value estimates in each case study, comparing to other explanation methods.
COST: 2073600
PREDICTION: We expect the case studies to provide compelling examples of the value of Shapley value estimation in real-world applications, but the development of meaningful case studies might require significant effort and collaboration with stakeholders in different domains.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Learning Branched Schrödinger Bridges for Temporal Population Dynamics
PROPOSAL: We train a graph neural network on real-world single-cell RNA-seq data to predict branched stochastic bridges between an initial and a target distribution of cell states. Specifically, we learn a discrete-time Markov model where each step represents a branching event, and the dynamics are informed by a learned energy function that balances the entropic cost of transiting between cell states and a task-specific state cost.
CONTROLS: We compare to standard Schrödinger bridge matching, generalized Schrödinger bridge, and a vanilla Diffusion-based model, as well as an ablation study on the importance of the branching mechanism.
COST: 1000
PREDICTION: We expect the branched Schrödinger bridge model to outperform existing methods in capturing branched cell-state trajectories, particularly for drug-perturbation responses in single-cell data. The model may struggle with overfitting when the initial and target distributions are highly multimodal, which could fail to generalize to unseen datasets.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Model Performance on Navigation and Cell Differentiation Domains
PROPOSAL: We evaluate our branched Schrödinger bridge model on two real-world datasets from different domains: a LiDAR-scanned terrain surface for navigation task, and a single-cell RNA-seq dataset for cell differentiation trajectory inference. This assessment helps establish the model's applicability and performance across distinct domains and tasks.
CONTROLS: Same baselines as in proposal 1, without the ablation study due to computational resource constraints.
COST: 1200
PREDICTION: We expect the model to perform reasonably well on the cell differentiation task, capturing branched trajectories in cell-state transitions. Due to the fundamentally different nature of the LiDAR terrain surface, we anticipate performance to be lower, but still competitive with existing methods, particularly at capturing the high-level structure of optimal navigation paths.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Analyzing Mode Collapse in Branched Schrödinger Bridges
PROPOSAL: We conduct a set of experiments on synthetic branched distributions to analyze how our branched Schrödinger bridge model handles mode collapse, comparing mode counting estimates between particles transported through independent stochastic trajectories (to which our model is similar in spirit) and through the learned branched dynamics. We evaluate performance under varying branching probabilities and particle counts.
CONTROLS: Same baselines as in proposal 1 (although this time without the ablation study).
COST: 1500
PREDICTION: By leveraging branched dynamics, we anticipate our model will exhibit improved resistance to mode collapse, resulting in more accurate mode counting estimates, particularly when the branching probability or particle count is increased. Performance may degrade for very high branching probabilities, as this leads to more frequent and rapid splitting of mass across distinct modes, increasing the likelihood of particles drifting away from their target modes.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Analyzing Mode Collapse in Branched Schrödinger Bridges
PROPOSAL: We revise proposal 3 to include a novel KL-regularization term on the learned branching probabilities, optimizing to favor a smoother distribution of mass across branches. This adaptation should further reduce mode collapse, and we test its efficacy by assessing particle counts and mode occupation frequencies in both the branched and single-trajectory (baseline) cases.
CONTROLS: Same baselines as in proposal 1 (without the ablation study).
COST: 1800
PREDICTION: By incorporating KL-regularization, we expect to see a significant reduction in mode collapse for our branched Schrödinger bridge model, leading to more accurate mode counting estimates even when branching probabilities are increased. The regularization term may, however, impose an unwanted mode smoothing effect when branching probabilities are very low, making it challenging to discern completely separate modes in the distribution.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Theoretical Guarantees for Branched Schrödinger Bridges
PROPOSAL: We establish theoretical convergence guarantees for our branched Schrödinger bridge model under certain conditions on the learned energy function. These results provide a theoretical foundation for the model's performance and highlight the importance of smooth, non-degenerate energy landscapes for capturing branched dynamics.
CONTROLS: None, as this is a theoretical proposal.
COST: 2000
PREDICTION: We expect to prove that under conditions of Lipschitz continuity and strong convexity of the energy function, our model converges to a stable, physically plausible branched distribution, with the rate of convergence depending on the strength of these conditions. This result may fail to hold for very high-dimensional state spaces or highly noisy energy measurements, where the convergence guarantees may degenerate due to the curse of dimensionality or noise-induced instability.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Smoothness-Constrained Learning for Branched Energy Functions
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel optimization algorithm that enforces smoothness constraints on the learned energy function, promoting a more physically plausible, non-degenerate distribution of mass across branches. Our algorithm is grounded in recent advances in non-convex optimization and can be applied to a broad class of energy-based models.
CONTROLS: Baselines similar to proposal 1, with an emphasis on comparing our smoothness-constrained approach to unconstrained optimization.
COST: 2200
PREDICTION: We expect that by enforcing smoothness constraints, our algorithm will improve upon the performance of unconstrained optimization, both qualitatively (capturing more realistic branched dynamics) and quantitatively (improving metrics such as mode counting accuracy). In certain cases, imposing smoothness constraints too aggressively may still hinder the model's ability to capture non-smooth features of the true energy landscape.

ACTION: REVISE 5
TITLE: Smoothness-Constrained Learning for Branched Energy Functions
PROPOSAL: We revise our smoothness-constrained learning algorithm to incorporate a mechanism for adaptively balancing smoothness constraints against the model's ability to capture non-smooth features of the true energy landscape. This adaptive adjustment is achieved through a meta-learning component that optimizes hyperparameters for smoothness regularization based on the dataset's inherent geometry.
CONTROLS: Same baselines as before, plus an evaluation of the adaptive smoothness-constrained approach against a fixed-smoothness approach.
COST: 2500
PREDICTION: By adaptively tuning smoothness constraints, we expect our algorithm to strike a better balance between physical plausibility and accurate capture of branched dynamics, potentially leading to improved performance on downstream tasks. However, the increased complexity of adaptive smoothness constraints may introduce additional challenges in optimizing the model's parameters, particularly in high-dimensional or noisy settings.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Bridging the Gap to Real-World Single-Cell Data with Unsupervised Validation
PROPOSAL: We incorporate an unsupervised validation strategy to improve the model's ability to generalize to real-world single-cell RNA-seq datasets with sparse or noisy annotations. This involves learning a proxy task on the target dataset to predict cell-state similarities, helping the model refine its branched dynamics to better match the underlying biology.

ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Unsupervised Graph Intrinsic Deformation (UGID) for test-time OOD detection
PROPOSAL: We propose UGID, a novel method to adapt a pre-trained GNN for test-time OOD detection. At test time, UGID distorts the input graph in an unsupervised manner by iteratively and locally warping its topology, effectively removing structural redundancy. The distorted graph is then fed into the pre-trained GNN, which outputs a score for the probability of the graph being OOD. We use a strong baseline of the GOODAT method and also compare against an ablation of UGID where no warping is performed (UGID-w).
CONTROLS: UGID vs. GOODAT; UGID-w vs. GOODAT
COST: 30000
PREDICTION: UGID will perform better than GOODAT by 5-10% in OOD detection accuracy on molecular property prediction and social network analysis tasks, but may struggle on protein function classification task due to complex topological structures in protein graphs, leading to potential over-warping in UGID.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Substructure-aware Anomaly Scoring (SAS) for test-time OOD detection
PROPOSAL: We propose SAS, a method that partitions the input graph into a set of disjoint subgraphs using a pre-trained graph clustering model. Anomaly scores for each subgraph are then computed using a set of pre-defined subgraph-level features and a learned similarity metric between the subgraph features and the features of known ID subgraphs. The final OOD score for the graph is computed as a weighted sum of the subgraph-level anomaly scores. We compare SAS against UGID and GOODAT on a range of tasks.
CONTROLS: SAS vs. UGID; SAS vs. GOODAT; UGID vs. GOODAT
COST: 45000
PREDICTION: SAS will outperform UGID on tasks with complex graph structures (e.g. protein function classification) due to its ability to capture subgraph-level anomalies, but may be outperformed by UGID on tasks with relatively simple graph structures (e.g. molecular property prediction) due to the additional computational overhead of subgraph partitioning.
